data.title: The Lost Lake Photograph
data.historicalImageCredit: University of Melbourne historical material; final image credit to be confirmed when the chosen archive image is uploaded.
data.buildingStory: Union Lawn remains one of the central outdoor gathering spaces on the Parkville campus. Its present lawns, paving and surrounding buildings conceal an older water landscape beneath the modern campus.
data.prototypeDesign: A small sepia photograph card with worn paper edges, showing the former campus lake. The reverse can carry a simple map mark linking the lost water feature to the present-day Union Lawn.
data.historicalStory: Before the present Union Lawn took shape, this part of the Parkville campus contained a wet area that became an ornamental lake. The lake was gradually filled as the campus expanded, beginning around the construction of the New Chemistry Building in the late 1930s, and the reclaimed area eventually became the Union Lawn, also known as the Concrete Lawn.
data.clue: This busy lawn was not always dry ground. Find the place where a campus lake slowly disappeared beneath today's meeting space.
data.sourceTitle: Union Lawn / Concrete Lawn — Constructing Change: the evolving Parkville campus
data.shortDescription: A digital relic recalling the ornamental lake that once occupied today's Union Lawn.
data.coordinateSource: MAP-ASSISTED DEVELOPMENT ESTIMATE (2026-10-05): player standing point (-37.797149,144.961958) selected within University Plaza / Concrete Lawn using the University of Melbourne University Plaza POI, Google Maps satellite imagery, and official Constructing Change material linking the former lake to Union Lawn. Intended photo view is approximately 288 degrees magnetic toward a wide west-northwest view of the former-lake area. Not field surveyed; final GPS and heading calibration remain pending.

data.title: The Surviving Stone Rosette
data.historicalImageCredit: University of Melbourne Archives / Constructing Change.
data.buildingStory: Wilson Hall has long served as a ceremonial centre for the University, hosting graduations, examinations, concerts and other major events. The present building was designed by Bates, Smart and McCutcheon and officially opened in March 1956.
data.prototypeDesign: A palm-sized reconstruction of a weathered stone rosette. The surface should look slightly fire-darkened and worn, suggesting an architectural fragment that survived the destruction of the earlier hall.
data.historicalStory: The first Wilson Hall opened in 1882 and became a major Gothic landmark of the University. On 25 January 1952, a fire destroyed the roof and badly damaged the hall. The replacement Wilson Hall opened in 1956 in a modern post-war style, while retaining links to the earlier building through surviving elements including stone rosettes.
data.clue: A fire destroyed the old hall, but not every piece of stone vanished. Search around the ceremonial building that rose in its place.
data.sourceTitle: Wilson Hall, 1956 — Constructing Change: the evolving Parkville campus
data.shortDescription: A miniature stone rosette inspired by surviving architectural elements from the original Gothic Wilson Hall.
data.coordinateSource: MAP-ASSISTED DEVELOPMENT ESTIMATE (2026-10-05): player standing point (-37.797895,144.961417) selected on the north-side approach to Wilson Hall using University of Melbourne north-entrance guidance, mapped entrance geometry, satellite/map references, and the main-entrance sculpture as the observation target. Intended observation heading is approximately 197 degrees magnetic. Not field surveyed; final GPS, sightline and heading calibration remain pending.

data.title: Miniature Fossil Specimen
data.historicalImageCredit: University of Melbourne Old Quad / source material relating to Arthur Bartholomew, Ludwig Becker and Frederick McCoy.
data.sourceTitle: Towards a glass monument — Old Quad, University of Melbourne
data.buildingStory: Old Quad is the University's original building and sits at the historic centre of the Parkville campus. Its restored north wing now brings together nineteenth-century architecture with contemporary exhibitions and the large stained-glass work at the northern entrance.
data.prototypeDesign: A small sandstone-coloured fossil slab with a raised fern imprint. The object should look like a museum specimen rather than a polished souvenir, linking the treasure directly to the fossil imagery in the stained glass.
data.historicalStory: The stained-glass work Towards a glass monument at Old Quad was developed from two early drawings of Mesozoic ferns fossilised in sandstone. The drawings were made by Arthur Bartholomew and Ludwig Becker and survive through lithographs in Frederick McCoy's Prodromus. The modern glass work reinterprets those scientific images as part of the University's architectural and research history.
data.clue: At the University's oldest building, prehistoric plant forms reappear in modern glass. Look near the northern entrance.
data.shortDescription: A pocket-sized fossil replica inspired by the Mesozoic fern imagery behind Old Quad's stained-glass installation.
data.coordinateSource: Google Maps Old Quadrangle place marker (-37.7975919,144.9609685), rounded to 5 decimals; official north-entry description and campus plan used to select the north-wing vicinity. Place marker, NOT a Google-labelled doorway or surveyed exterior threshold.

data.title: Reconstructed Miniature Atlas Figure
data.historicalImageCredit: University of Melbourne; final image credit to be confirmed for the selected Atlas reference photograph.
data.buildingStory: The South Lawn Car Park opened in 1972 and was an unusual fully underground car park beneath a landscaped lawn. Its dramatic concrete interior and reused architectural elements have made it one of the University's most distinctive spaces and a location used in film and television.
data.prototypeDesign: A small grey stone-effect Atlas figure reconstructed as a freestanding miniature. Keep the figure and the globe-like load in the same muted stone colour so it reads as a fragment of the historic entrance rather than a bright fantasy statue.
data.historicalStory: The two Atlas figures at the western entrance originally belonged to the Colonial Bank of Australasia in central Melbourne. After that building was demolished, the figures were preserved and later incorporated into the South Lawn Car Park entrance, giving the modern underground structure a striking link to nineteenth-century Melbourne.
data.clue: Below the lawn, two stone giants appear to carry an impossible weight. Find the entrance where they still stand guard.
data.sourceTitle: Myer launches new season collection in iconic University of Melbourne car park — University of Melbourne Newsroom
data.shortDescription: A miniature reconstruction of one of the Atlas figures framing the western entrance to the South Lawn Car Park.

data.title: Miniature Glasshouse Model
data.historicalImageCredit: University of Melbourne Sustainable Campus; final historical image credit to be confirmed when selected.
data.sourceTitle: The System Garden — Sustainable Campus, University of Melbourne
data.buildingStory: The System Garden is one of Australia's oldest teaching gardens. Its layout, plant collections and surviving glasshouse tower preserve the University's long connection between botanical teaching, classification and living collections.
data.prototypeDesign: A delicate tabletop model of the former octagonal conservatory, with a solid central tower and transparent glass-like panels around it. The model should make the missing glasshouse visually understandable at a glance.
data.historicalStory: The System Garden was established in 1856 as a teaching garden arranged to help students compare plant groups. Its central tower was originally the potting shed for a distinctive octagonal conservatory. The glasshouse itself was dismantled in 1916, leaving the tower as the surviving trace of the earlier structure.
data.clue: Only the centre remains. Imagine the glass walls that once wrapped around the old tower in this teaching garden.
data.shortDescription: A miniature reconstruction of the octagonal glasshouse that once surrounded the surviving central tower in the System Garden.
data.coordinateSource: Google Maps pin drop at System Garden (-37.7966124089,144.959126948), address label -37.796612, 144.959127. Map-based development estimate; not field surveyed.

data.title: Miniature Kangaroo-Pouch Tone-Tool Model
data.historicalImageCredit: Grainger Museum, University of Melbourne. Object identifier 00.0216.
data.buildingStory: The Grainger Museum preserves instruments, documents and experimental machines connected with Percy Grainger's musical ideas. The tone-tool reflects his effort to turn unconventional mechanical and electronic systems into new ways of shaping sound.
data.prototypeDesign: A compact mechanical-looking miniature with a timber-coloured frame, small rollers, paper-strip details and simplified wires or gears. It should read as an experimental sound machine rather than a conventional musical instrument.
data.historicalStory: Percy Grainger and Burnett Cross built the Kangaroo-pouch tone-tool in 1952 as part of Grainger's experiments in Free Music. The original machine used a large wooden frame, paper rolls and oscillator-based electronics in an attempt to control continuously changing pitch and musical movement.
data.clue: Look for a machine built to make pitch move freely rather than step from note to note. Paper, rollers and oscillators are the key.
data.shortDescription: A miniature model inspired by Percy Grainger and Burnett Cross's 1952 Kangaroo-pouch tone-tool.
